title: Lattice Launches Quantum-Resistant Security Stack for AI Data Centres
excerpt: Lattice Sentry 5.0 adds post-quantum cryptography to firmware protection and attestation for AI infrastructure, pairing Lattice FPGAs with AMI software in a CNSA 2.0-aligned package.
body:
• Lattice Sentry 5.0 is billed as the first platform firmware resilience and attestation stack enabled for post-quantum cryptography.
  • The stack protects BIOS, baseboard management controllers and other board firmware, with detection and autonomous recovery aligned to NIST SP 800-193.
  • It combines Lattice's CNSA 2.0-compliant FPGAs with AMI's platform software, using ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS for authentication and ML-KEM for key exchange.
  • Demo boards and design services are available now, and Lattice will show the system at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose on October 13-15.

Lattice Semiconductor has moved quantum-resistant security from its chips to a complete platform stack for AI data centres. The San Jose-based company, listed on Nasdaq as LSCC, announced Lattice Sentry solution stack version 5.0 on October 12, describing it as the industry's first post-quantum cryptography-enabled platform firmware resilience and attestation solution.

The release extends Lattice's work on post-quantum cryptography from silicon to the full platform, with protection aligned to the NSA's CNSA 2.0 suite and to NIST standards. For system designers, Lattice says, that offers a validated and production-ready route to quantum-resistant security across AI data centres and critical infrastructure, rather than a set of parts to assemble themselves. Its official site is at latticesemi.com.

Why firmware, and why now

Firmware sits below the operating system and controls how a server boots and is managed, which makes it a valuable target: compromise it, and higher-level defences may never see the intrusion. Mamta Gupta, Lattice's vice president for business development in compute and communications, put it plainly in the announcement: "Platform firmware has become a primary attack vector."

https://x.com/iotex_io/status/2109683234867167568

The quantum argument is about timing rather than an attack that has already arrived. Hardware deployed in data centres today can stay in service for years, and cryptographic standards take time to replace. Lattice's position is that operators should not have to choose between protection against current threats and readiness for quantum-era attacks that could undermine long-standing security assumptions. Building post-quantum methods in now, while classical cryptography remains supported, is the company's answer.

What the stack includes

The firmware resilience layer covers BIOS, baseboard management controllers and other board firmware, with protection, detection and autonomous recovery aligned to NIST SP 800-193. It adds crypto-agility with anti-rollback protection, secure firmware updates, key provisioning and revocation, and secure decommissioning at the end of a system's life.

For cryptography, the stack supports CNSA 2.0-compliant post-quantum algorithms: ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS for authentication, ML-KEM for key exchange, and LMS and XMSS hash-based signature verification. Classical methods remain available, including ECDSA and AES-GCM, so existing designs are not forced into an abrupt switch.

Identity and attestation form the third layer. The stack uses SPDM-based device attestation across servers and rack infrastructure, DICE-anchored cryptographic identity and measurement to support supply-chain and platform integrity, and multi-device attestation designed for disaggregated rack environments. It pairs Lattice's CNSA 2.0-compliant FPGA portfolio with AMI's platform management software, including the AMI Tektagon framework for provisioning, attestation, firmware updates and lifecycle management.

From evaluation to production

Lattice is selling Sentry as a path rather than a component. The package includes a validated reference platform, an IP library, its Radiant and Propel design tools alongside AMI Tektagon, and ready-to-run demonstrations. Demo boards and custom design services are available now, the company said.

The timing puts the product in front of its target buyers this week. Lattice will display Sentry and its other post-quantum products at the OCP Global Summit 2026, running October 13-15 at the San Jose Convention Center, at booths A53-A54. Planned demonstrations cover firmware resiliency, flash-less boot architectures, rack-scale management and telemetry, quantum-resistant security and AI-enabled sensor aggregation.

What to watch

For Indian and diaspora engineers who build and run cloud and AI infrastructure in the United States, the practical question is adoption: whether server makers integrate a pre-validated stack like Sentry into shipping platforms, and how quickly data-centre operators make post-quantum firmware protection a purchasing requirement. Standards alignment helps that case, but procurement decisions will turn on cost, performance and how smoothly the stack fits existing management tools. Sentry 5.0 gives Lattice an early, complete offer in that contest — the test now is design wins, not announcements.
